title: Two Sum
description: Find two numbers in an array that add up to a target value. Compare brute-force, hash map, and two-pointer approaches.

data.text: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`.
You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.
Check every pair of numbers. For each element, look ahead to see if its complement exists.

data.title: Brute Force O(n²) — Baseline
Why this is O(n²)
data.text: For each of the n elements, we potentially scan all remaining elements. The nested loop creates n * (n-1) / 2 comparisons in the worst case.
Store each number's index as we iterate. For each new number, check if its complement (target - num) was already seen.

data.title: Hash Map O(n) — Optimal
What improved here?
data.text: **Time:** Reduced from O(n²) to O(n) by trading memory for speed. The dictionary provides O(1) lookups. **Space:** Increased from O(1) to O(n) to store the map. This is the standard interview-optimal solution.
If we sort the array first, we can use two pointers — one at the start, one at the end — and move them inward based on the sum.

data.title: Two-Pointer O(n log n) — Note: requires sorted input
Trade-off
data.text: This approach is O(n log n) due to sorting. It's useful when the input is already sorted, but for unsorted arrays, the hash map one-pass approach is faster. Also note that sorting scrambles indices, so we must track original indices.

cards.title: Brute Force
cons: O(n²) time — too slow for large inputs

cards.title: Two-Pointer (Sorted)
cards.description: Sort then scan from both ends
cons: Worse than hash map for unsorted
